draft.title: Scale
card: Scale is the size of the area a geographer looks at. Four common scales are local, regional, national and global.
local is a small area, such as a suburb or a creek. Regional is a larger area made of many localities, such as a river catchment or the Darling Downs in Queensland.
national is a whole country, such as Australia. Global is the whole Earth, or issues that cross many countries.
The same issue can look different at each scale. An explanation that fits at one scale may not fit at another, so geographers often check more than one.
draft.remember: Look at an issue at more than one scale, because what you find can change with the scale.

a.q: Which of these studies of rainfall is set at a regional scale?
opts: Rainfall across the Murray-Darling Basin over ten years
Rainfall that collects in one school oval after a storm
Average rainfall for Australia as a single country
Rainfall patterns for every continent on Earth
a.why: A river basin is a large area made of many localities, so it is regional. A playground is local, a whole country is national and every continent is global.
a.clue: Think of an area bigger than a suburb but smaller than a country.

b.q: Dana finds her town's average temperature has stayed steady for 20 years. A national study shows Australia warming over the same time. What does this best show about scale?
opts: The same issue can show a different pattern at each scale
Two studies of one issue should agree if both are done well
A local study is too small to tell geographers anything
The national trend will show up in each town's records
b.why: The same issue can look different at each scale, so a steady town and a warming country can both be correct. The tempting idea that well-done studies should agree assumes the scales must match, but a pattern at one scale may not fit at another.
b.clue: Both results could be true at their own scale.
